**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Time allowed: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section. All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples. Only the required number of questions will be marked. Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Structure of the paper: SECTION A: Physical Geography (questions 1 to 3); SECTION B: Human Geography (questions 4 to 6); SECTION C: Contemporary Environmental and Development Issues (question 7, with an EITHER/OR choice between two sets of sub-questions).

questions.enonce_markdown: (a) Examine the influence of climate and parent material on soil characteristics.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Soil is formed by the interaction of several factors: climate, parent material, relief, organisms (vegetation, soil fauna) and time. Climate and parent material are the two most important: climate controls the *processes* that act on the soil, and parent material supplies the *minerals* from which it is made. Soil characteristics include **depth, texture, structure, colour, pH, nutrient content, humus content and drainage**.

**1. Influence of climate.**
- *Temperature and moisture control weathering and biological activity.* In the hot, humid tropics, chemical weathering is deep and fast and organic matter decomposes quickly. In cold or dry climates weathering and decomposition are slow, so soils are thin and, in cold climates, rich in undecomposed humus.
- *Rainfall controls leaching and the movement of water.* Where rainfall exceeds evaporation, soluble minerals and bases are leached downwards (**eluviation**) and the soil becomes acidic. In the equatorial forest zone of southern Cameroon, heavy rain and heat lead to **ferrallitic soils**: deep, red or yellow (iron and aluminium oxides remain while silica and bases are washed out), acidic and low in nutrients, with a thin humus layer because the litter decomposes rapidly and the nutrients are taken up at once by the forest (a nearly closed nutrient cycle).
- *In dry climates*, evaporation exceeds rainfall and water moves upwards by capillary action, depositing salts and lime near the surface (**salinisation** or calcification); soils are shallow, alkaline and low in humus, with little weathering. In the savanna, alternating wet and dry seasons give iron-rich crusts (laterite) in places.
- *Temperate climates* with cool, moist summers give **podzols** under coniferous forest (strong leaching, acid humus) and brown earths under deciduous forest.
- Climate therefore governs the **zonal** pattern of soils across the world (large-scale zones of soil that follow climatic and vegetation belts).

**2. Influence of parent material.**
- *Mineral content and chemical composition.* Basic igneous rocks such as basalt weather to clay-rich soils rich in calcium, magnesium and potassium: the **volcanic soils** of the slopes of Mount Cameroon and of the Western Highlands are dark, deep and fertile and support dense farming. Granite and sandstones, rich in silica (quartz), give acidic, sandy, leached soils with fewer nutrients. Limestone gives calcareous soils (rendzinas) that are alkaline and thin.
- *Texture and permeability.* Sandy parent materials give coarse, well-drained, light soils with low water-holding capacity; clays give fine-textured, heavy and often poorly drained soils; in the Lake Chad basin, in the north of Cameroon, the clay-rich **vertisols** (the "karal" soils) swell when wet and crack when dry.
- *Colour, depth and pH* also reflect the parent material, especially in **young soils**, where time has been too short for climate to erase the rock's influence.

**3. Relative importance and interaction.** On a large scale climate is dominant, as ferrallitic soils form on many different parent rocks in the humid tropics (the parent material has been transformed). On a small or local scale, or in young or cool-climate soils, parent material is dominant and gives local (intrazonal and azonal) soils such as those developed on volcanic ash, alluvium or limestone. Climate and parent material also work through other factors: they determine the vegetation which supplies humus, and relief affects drainage and erosion.

**Conclusion.** Climate controls the rate and type of weathering, leaching and organic matter decomposition, and parent material controls the mineral composition, texture and drainage; together they explain the contrast between fertile volcanic soils, leached acid forest soils and the clay or sandy soils of the savanna.

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) Describe the stages involved in plant succession.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Definition.** Plant succession is the sequence of changes in the plant community of an area over time, as each community modifies the environment (soil, light, moisture) and is then replaced by another, until a stable, self-perpetuating community (the **climax**) is reached. The whole sequence is a **sere**, and each stage a **seral stage**. **Primary succession** starts on a new, bare surface (rock, sand, water, volcanic ash); **secondary succession** starts after an existing community has been destroyed (for example by fire or farming) while soil remains.

**The general stages.**

1. **Colonisation (pioneer stage).** Hardy pioneer species, tolerant of harsh conditions, arrive as spores or seeds carried by wind, water or animals: bacteria, algae, lichens and mosses on bare rock; marram or salt-tolerant grasses on dunes and mud. They have few needs, grow quickly and reproduce in large numbers. They begin to break down the rock and accumulate a little organic matter. Biodiversity and biomass are low.
2. **Establishment and competition (intermediate stages, seral stages).** The pioneers' remains form humus; a thin soil develops that holds water and nutrients, so grasses, herbs and then shrubs establish themselves, more species arrive, and the pioneers are shaded out and replaced. Species diversity, biomass and soil depth increase. Taller species outcompete the earlier ones for light, water and nutrients.
3. **Stabilisation (the woody stage).** Shrubs are followed by fast-growing pioneer trees and then by long-lived forest trees. The soil is deeper, richer and has a litter layer, and the microclimate is more humid and shaded. Shade-tolerant species begin to take the place of the light-demanding species.
4. **Climax.** The community is in equilibrium with climate and soil: diversity and biomass are high, nutrients are cycled efficiently, and further change is slow. This is the **climatic climax** (such as tropical rainforest in the equatorial climate, savanna grassland and woodland in the tropical wet-dry climate). If human activity (fire, grazing, farming) holds the community at a stage short of the climatic climax, it is a **plagioclimax**.

**Examples of seres.**
- **Lithosere (bare rock):** bare rock - lichens and mosses - grasses and herbs - shrubs - trees (climax woodland).
- **Hydrosere (fresh water):** open water - submerged plants - floating-leaved plants - reed swamp - sedge and fen - shrubs (carr) - climax woodland. Sediment and plant remains slowly fill the pond.
- **Psammosere (sand dunes)** and **halosere (salt marsh, mangrove):** in the mangrove swamps of the coastal estuaries (for example the Wouri estuary), tolerant mangrove species stabilise the mud and later species colonise the higher, drier areas.
- **Secondary succession on abandoned farmland (fallow) in the forest zone of southern Cameroon:** weeds and herbs - grasses and shrubs - fast-growing pioneer trees (such as the umbrella tree, *Musanga cecropioides*) - young secondary forest - mature forest after many decades.

**Trends along the succession.** Species diversity, biomass, soil depth and humus, nutrient cycling and the complexity of the food web increase; the species that dominate change from small, fast-growing (r-strategy) to large, long-lived (K-strategy) forms; pioneers are replaced.

**Conclusion.** Succession proceeds from colonisation by pioneers, through intermediate stages in which the vegetation changes the environment and is itself replaced, to a stable climax community in balance with climate and soil, unless interrupted by natural or human disturbance.

*(A labelled diagram of a sere, such as a hydrosere or lithosere, earns the diagram marks.)*
